alienate

AY-lee-uh-nayt -- four syllables, stress on the first syllable, AY. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To alienate is to isolate, cut off, or divide.

His constant bragging began to alienate even his oldest friends.

Example

The new club president redesigns the logo, cancels the annual picnic, and changes the meeting night -- all without asking anyone. Within two months, attendance drops from thirty members to nine, and the nine who remain sit in the back exchanging looks.

The president has alienated the members: cut them off and pushed them away from a group they once felt part of. You alienate people who used to be on your side -- the word describes turning belonging into distance, usually without meaning to.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

repel: To repel is to drive someone back or away on the spot -- rudeness or a bad smell repels instantly. To alienate works far more slowly: it turns people who were once on your side into outsiders, cooling their loyalty over weeks rather than pushing them back in a moment.

offend: To offend is to sting someone's feelings in the moment -- a rude joke offends, and a sincere apology can patch it up by evening. To alienate cuts deeper and lasts longer: offended people are angry tonight, while people you alienate stop feeling they belong with you at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unite: to bring together as one

befriend: to make a friend of someone

Where it sits · how completely the bond breaks — distance → alienate → estrange

distance vs. alienate: To distance people is simply to cool the connection a little, while to alienate them is to push them out of the circle entirely -- they no longer feel they belong.

estrange vs. alienate: Estrange is the strongest and most personal: alienated voters may still come back next election, but estranged relatives have let the bond itself break, often for years.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — alien-

root — alien-: belonging to another; foreign (Latin alienus, from alius 'other')

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make, to cause to be (Latin -atus)

Put it together

Put it together: Alienate comes from Latin alienus, 'belonging to another,' from alius, 'other.' To alienate people is literally to make them other -- to take someone who belonged with you and turn them into an outsider. The science-fiction 'alien' is the same root wearing a spacesuit.

Use the root in a new word: alien

Use the root in a new word: alien: Inspectors screen the harbor for alien species carried in on the hulls of ships.

Root Check

Word Choice

Alienate takes people as its object -- you alienate friends, voters, customers, teammates -- and it almost always describes an unintended result: the bragging, the price hike, or the sarcasm does the alienating. Watch for the pattern 'alienate the very people you need,' one of the word's most common shapes in test passages.
